1.title: Explicit Criteria and Few-Shot Prompting
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: Explicit Criteria and Few-Shot Prompting. This module covers task statements four point one and four point two: explicit criteria and few-shot prompting. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Why explicit criteria beat vague instructions and "be conservative". How false positives destroy developer trust, and what to do about them. Severity criteria with concrete code examples. Few-shot examples: when, how many, and what they should show.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply's Review Bot Cries Wolf
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply's Review Bot Cries Wolf. The C I review bot comments on every pull request. Developers say "half the comments are noise" and have started ignoring all of them, including the real security findings. The prompt says: "Review the code and report issues. Be conservative; only report high-confidence findings.".

1.title: Explicit Criteria Beat Vague Instructions
1.text: Explicit Criteria Beat Vague Instructions. "Check that comments are accurate". "Flag a comment only when the behavior it claims contradicts what the code actually does". "Be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings". "Report: bugs and security vulnerabilities. Skip: minor style and local naming patterns". "Rate how severe it is". A severity table with a short code example for each level.

1.title: Explicit Criteria Beat Vague Instructions, continued
1.text: Explicit Criteria Beat Vague Instructions, continued. The figure shows this: Replace general instructions with categorical criteria: what to report, what to skip, and how to rate severity. General phrases such as "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" do not improve precision: the model cannot calibrate "confidence" the way you imagine. Specific, categorical criteria do. False positives are costly beyond the noise. A category with a high false-positive rate undermines trust in the accurate categories too.

1.title: Explicit Criteria Beat Vague Instructions, continued
1.text: Explicit Criteria Beat Vague Instructions, continued. If one category is noisy, temporarily disable it to restore trust while you improve its prompt, then re-enable it. Severity levels need definitions and examples: for each level give a short concrete code example, so classification is consistent from run to run.

1.title: Explicit Criteria Beat Vague Instructions, continued
1.text: Explicit Criteria Beat Vague Instructions, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: Asked how to reduce false positives? to specific criteria for what to report and skip, not "be more conservative" and not a confidence cutoff. Exam tip: Severity that varies between runs needs a definition and a code example for each level.

1.title: Few-Shot Prompting
1.text: Few-Shot Prompting. Few-shot prompting puts a few worked examples of input and desired output in the prompt. Get consistent format. When detailed instructions still give inconsistent output, examples are the most effective technique. Show ambiguous cases. Examples of tool selection for ambiguous requests, or branch-level test-coverage gaps. Generalize judgment. Models apply the reasoning to novel patterns, not only to the examples listed. Reduce hallucination in extraction. Show handling of informal measurements and varied document structures.

1.title: Few-Shot Prompting, continued
1.text: Few-Shot Prompting, continued. The figure shows this: A good few-shot example shows the input, the exact output format, and the reasoning for the choice. How many: two to four targeted examples, aimed at the ambiguous situations (not easy cases). Show the reasoning: state why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives. Show the output format: location, issue, severity, suggested fix.

1.title: Few-Shot Prompting, continued
1.text: Few-Shot Prompting, continued. Contrast acceptable patterns with genuine issues so the model skips harmless code (fewer false positives) yet still generalizes. Varied document structures (inline citations versus a bibliography; methodology sections versus details embedded in text) to examples with each structure. Empty or null extraction of fields that exist in the source? Add examples from documents with varied formats showing the correct extraction. Exam tip: Instructions alone give inconsistent output to few-shot examples. But a missing-information problem (the document does not contain the data) is not fixed by examples; see Modules ten and eleven.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Explicit criteria: Say what to report and what to skip; categorical beats "be conservative" or confidence cutoffs. Contradiction example: Flag a comment only when its claim contradicts the code. False positives: Hurt trust in all categories; temporarily disable a noisy one while you fix the prompt. Severity: Define each level with a concrete code example. Few-shot: Best for consistent format and ambiguous cases; two to four targeted examples with reasoning. Few-shot extras: Show the target format; contrast acceptable versus genuine; varied document structures reduce empty extraction.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A review bot's developers ignore comments because many are false positives. The prompt says "only report high-confidence findings". What change is most effective? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Categorical criteria improve precision. General cautions and confidence filtering do not.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. One category (naming comments) has a sixty percent false-positive rate, while the security category is accurate. Developers have started ignoring everything. What is the best short-term step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Disabling a noisy category restores trust in the accurate ones while you fix it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Severity labels vary between runs: the same missing check is "medium" once and "critical" the next time. What is the best fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Examples per level anchor the classification and make it consistent.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Detailed written instructions still produce inconsistent report formatting. What technique is the most effective next? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Examples demonstrate the format that prose fails to convey.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. How many few-shot examples are typically best, and aimed at what? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A few well-chosen examples of the ambiguous situations teach judgment.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. An extraction prompt keeps returning empty values for "author" in documents where the author appears in different places. Which improvement fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Examples from varied structures help the model find the field wherever it appears.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. What is a benefit of including both acceptable code patterns and genuine issues in the examples? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Contrast examples teach the boundary between harmless and harmful code.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Select two. Which two changes most improve the precision of a review prompt? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Categorical criteria and severity examples change what is reported. Vague caution and confidence filtering do not.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: C. Question two: A. Question three: A. Question four: C. Question five: B. Question six: C. Question seven: D. Question eight: C and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
